claim: The brain integrates visual and vestibular cues to infer heading-direction in an optimal way as predicted by Bayesian inference.
source: Indeed, experimental data has shown that the brain does integrate visual and vestibular cues to infer heading-direction and furthermore, the brain does it in an optimal way as predicted by Bayesian inference (Fetsch et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fetsch et al., 2013

claim: Optimal information integration has been found among many sensory modalities including visual and auditory cues for inferring object location.
source: Over the past years, experimental and theoretical studies verified that optimal information integration were found among many sensory modalities, for example, integration of visual and auditory cues for inferring object location (Alais and Burr, 2004), motion and texture cues for depth perception (Jacobs, 1999), visual and proprioceptive cues for hand position (van Beers et al., 1999), and visual and haptic cues for object height (Ernst and Banks, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental and theoretical studies

claim: Multisensory integration inevitably incurs information loss of individual cues.
source: An accompanying consequence of multisensory integration is, however, that it inevitably incurs information loss of individual cues (Figure 1, also see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and mathematical analysis in Materials and methods

claim: The amount of lost information increases with the extent of integration.
source: Thus, if only multisensory integration is performed, the brain faces a chicken and egg dilemma in stimulus perception: without integrating cues, it may be unable to recognize stimuli reliably in an ambiguous environment; but once cues are integrated, the information from individual cues is lost. Concurrent multisensory integration and segregation is able to disentangle this dilemma. The information of individual cues can be recovered by using the preserved disparity information if necessary, instead of re-gathering new inputs from the external world.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the integration process and is also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The brain can still sense the difference between cues in multisensory integration.
source: This processing scheme is consistent with an experimental finding which showed that the brain can still sense the difference between cues in multisensory integration (Wallace et al., 2004; Girshick and Banks, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: In MSTd and VIP, there are two types of neurons with comparable number displaying different multisensory behaviors: congruent and opposite cells.
source: Previous studies investigating the integration of visual and vestibular cues to infer heading-direction found that in each of two brain areas, namely, the dorsal medial superior temporal area (MSTd) and the ventral intraparietal area (VIP), there are two types of neurons with comparable number displaying different multisensory behaviors: congruent and opposite cells (Figure 2) (Gu et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies and illustrated in Figure 2

claim: The tuning curves of a congruent cell in response to visual and vestibular cues are similar.
source: The tuning curves of a congruent cell in response to visual and vestibular cues are similar (Figure 2A), whereas the tuning curve of an opposite cell in response to a visual cue is shifted by 180 degrees (half of the period) compared to that in response to a vestibular cue (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The tuning curve of an opposite cell in response to a visual cue is shifted by 180 degrees compared to that in response to a vestibular cue.
source: The tuning curves of a congruent cell in response to visual and vestibular cues are similar (Figure 2A), whereas the tuning curve of an opposite cell in response to a visual cue is shifted by 180 degrees (half of the period) compared to that in response to a vestibular cue (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Congruent neurons are responsible for cue integration.
source: Data analysis and modeling studies suggested that congruent neurons are responsible for cue integration (Gu et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to data analysis and modeling studies

claim: The computational role of opposite neurons remains largely unknown.
source: However, the computational role of opposite neurons remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Opposite neurons do not integrate cues as their responses hardly change when a single cue is replaced by two cues with similar directions.
source: They do not integrate cues as their responses hardly change when a single cue is replaced by two cues with similar directions.
evidence: This is based on observed neuronal response properties

claim: Opposite neurons' responses vary significantly when the disparity between visual and vestibular cues is enlarged.
source: Interestingly, however, their responses vary significantly when the disparity between visual and vestibular cues is enlarged (Morgan et al., 2008), indicating that opposite neurons are associated with the disparity information between cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Morgan et al., 2008

claim: Opposite neurons are associated with the disparity information between cues.
source: Interestingly, however, their responses vary significantly when the disparity between visual and vestibular cues is enlarged (Morgan et al., 2008), indicating that opposite neurons are associated with the disparity information between cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that opposite neurons respond to cue disparity

claim: Many brain areas exhibit multisensory processing behaviors and these areas are intensively and reciprocally connected with each other.
source: Experimental findings showed that many, rather than a single, brain areas exhibit multisensory processing behaviors and that these areas are intensively and reciprocally connected with each other (Gu et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013; Gu et al., 2016; Boussaoud et al., 1990; Baizer et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental findings

claim: The architecture of multisensory areas is consistent with the structure of a decentralized model.
source: The architecture of these multisensory areas is consistent with the structure of a decentralized model (Zhang et al., 2016), where information integration naturally emerges through the interactions between distributed network modules and is robust to local failure (Gu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to modeling studies

claim: The decentralized model successfully reproduces almost all known phenomena observed in the multisensory integration experiments.
source: The decentralized model successfully reproduces almost all known phenomena observed in the multisensory integration experiments (Fetsch et al., 2013; Stein and Stanford, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Congruent neurons in MSTd and VIP are reciprocally connected with each other in the congruent manner.
source: Specifically, we propose that congruent neurons in the two brain areas are reciprocally connected with each other in the congruent manner: the closer between the preferred directions over the feedforward cue of a pair of neurons in their respective brain areas, the stronger their connection is, and this connection profile encodes effectively the prior knowledge about the two cues coming from the same stimulus.
evidence: This is a proposed model architecture

claim: Opposite neurons in MSTd and VIP are reciprocally connected in the opposite manner.
source: On the other hand, opposite neurons in the two brain areas are reciprocally connected in the opposite manner: the further away between the preferred directions over the feedforward cue of a pair of neurons in their respective brain areas (the maximal difference is 180 degree), the stronger their connection is.
evidence: This is a proposed model architecture

claim: The model reproduces the tuning properties of opposite neurons.
source: Our model reproduces the tuning properties of opposite neurons, and verifies that opposite neurons encode the disparity information between cues.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model presented in the study

claim: Opposite neurons encode the disparity information between cues.
source: Our model reproduces the tuning properties of opposite neurons, and verifies that opposite neurons encode the disparity information between cues.
evidence: This is verified through the computational model

claim: The disparity information, in coordination with the integration result of congruent neurons, enables the neural system to assess the validity of cue integration.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that this disparity information, in coordination with the integration result of congruent neurons, enables the neural system to assess the validity of cue integration and to recover the lost information of individual cues if necessary.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the computational model

claim: The disparity information enables the neural system to recover the lost information of individual cues if necessary.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that this disparity information, in coordination with the integration result of congruent neurons, enables the neural system to assess the validity of cue integration and to recover the lost information of individual cues if necessary.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the computational model

claim: The posterior of stimulus s₁ given combined cues is equal to the product of the posteriors given the individual cues.
source: The above equation indicates that in multisensory integration, the posterior of a stimulus given combined cues is equal to the product of the posteriors given the individual cues.
evidence: This is derived from Bayesian inference mathematics (Equation 3)

claim: Optimal multisensory integration is equivalent to vector summation.
source: Thus, optimal multisensory integration is equivalent to vector summation (see Equation 4), with each vector representing the posterior of the stimulus given each cue (the sum of the two green vectors yields the blue vector in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation and illustrated in Figure 3B

claim: Multisensory segregation is interpreted as vector subtraction.
source: Similar to the geometrical interpretation of multisensory integration, multisensory segregation is interpreted as vector subtraction (the subtraction between two green vectors yields the red vector in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation and illustrated in Figure 3B

claim: When two vectors representing posteriors given individual cues have small disparity, the length of the summed vector is long and the length of the subtracted vector is short.
source: When the two vectors representing the posteriors given the individual cues have small disparity, that is the estimates from individual cues tend to support each other, the length of the summed vector is long, implying that the posterior of cue integration has a strong confidence, whereas the length of the subtracted vector is short, implying that the weak confidence of two cues are disparate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the geometric interpretation and shown in Figure 3D

claim: By comparing the lengths of the summed and subtracted vectors, the neural system can assess whether two cues should be integrated or segregated.
source: Thus, by comparing the lengths of the summed and subtracted vectors, the neural system can assess whether two cues should be integrated or segregated.
evidence: This is inferred from the geometric interpretation of integration and segregation

claim: The concentration of integration and disparity information changes with cue disparity in von Mises distribution.
source: A notable difference between von Mises distribution and Gaussian distribution is that the concentration of integration and disparity information changes with cue disparity in von Mises distribution (Figure 3D), while they are fixed in Gaussian distribution (Ernst, 2006).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and compared with Gaussian distribution from Ernst, 2006

claim: The tuning properties of congruent and opposite neurons naturally emerge through the network dynamics.
source: It shows that the congruent neuron, in response to either cue 1 or cue 2, prefers the same direction (−90°) (Figure 5A), whereas the opposite neuron, while preferring −90° for cue 1, prefers 90° for cue 2 (Figure 5B). Thus, the tuning properties of congruent and opposite neurons naturally emerge through the network dynamics.
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulations shown in Figure 5A-B

claim: When there is no disparity between two cues, the response of a congruent neuron is enhanced compared to the single cue conditions.
source: We further checked the responses of neurons to combined cues and found that when there is no disparity between the two cues, the response of a congruent neuron is enhanced compared to the single cue conditions (green line in Figure 5A), whereas the response of an opposite neuron is suppressed compared to its response to the direct cue (green line in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in network simulation results in Figure 5A

claim: When there is no disparity between two cues, the response of an opposite neuron is suppressed compared to its response to the direct cue.
source: We further checked the responses of neurons to combined cues and found that when there is no disparity between the two cues, the response of a congruent neuron is enhanced compared to the single cue conditions (green line in Figure 5A), whereas the response of an opposite neuron is suppressed compared to its response to the direct cue (green line in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in network simulation results in Figure 5B

claim: The network model's response properties agree with experimental data.
source: These properties agree with the experimental data (Gu et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013) and is also consistent with the interpretation that the integrated and segregated amplitudes are respectively proportional to the vector sum and difference in Figure 3.
evidence: The model results are compared with experimental data from cited studies

claim: The model reproduced the bimodal tuning curves of neurons in response to combined cues of varying reliability.
source: Following the experimental protocol (Morgan et al., 2008), we also plotted the bimodal tuning curves of the example neurons in response to the combined cues of varying reliability, and observed that when cue 1 has a relatively high reliability, the bimodal responses of both neurons are dominated by cue 1 (Figure 5C–D), indicating that the neuronal firing rates are affected more significantly by varying the angle of cue 1 than by that of cue 2, whereas when the reliability of cue 1 is reduced, the result becomes the opposite (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is shown in network simulation results in Figure 5C-F and compared with experimental protocol

claim: The model reproduced the distribution of intermediate neurons as observed in experiments.
source: We found that by considering the realistic imperfectness of neuronal reciprocal connections (e.g. adding random components in the reciprocal connections in Equations (18 and 19), see Materials and methods), our model reproduced the distribution of intermediate neurons as observed in the experiment (Figure 5G–H) (Gu et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in network simulation results in Figure 5G-H and compared with experimental data

claim: The network implements optimal integration and segregation.
source: Figure 6F–I indicates that the network indeed implements optimal integration and segregation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of network results with theoretical predictions in Figure 6F-I

claim: The input intensity encodes the reliability of the likelihood.
source: Moreover, comparing the network results with the results of the probabilistic model, we could find the analogy that the input intensity encodes the reliability of the likelihood (Equation 1, comparing Figure 6F with Figure 3C), and the reciprocal connection strength effectively represents the reliability of the integration prior (Equation 2, comparing Figure 6H with Figure 3E), which is consistent with a previous study (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing network results with probabilistic model predictions

claim: The reciprocal connection strength effectively represents the reliability of the integration prior.
source: Moreover, comparing the network results with the results of the probabilistic model, we could find the analogy that the input intensity encodes the reliability of the likelihood (Equation 1, comparing Figure 6F with Figure 3C), and the reciprocal connection strength effectively represents the reliability of the integration prior (Equation 2, comparing Figure 6H with Figure 3E), which is consistent with a previous study (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing network results with probabilistic model predictions

claim: The network model achieves cue integration and segregation robustly over a large range of parameters.
source: Our results indicated that the network model achieves cue integration and segregation robustly over a large range of parameters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), as long as the connection strengths are not so large that winner-take-all happens in the network model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic parameter variation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: The activity of congruent neurons decreases with cue disparity.
source: Figure 7A displays how the mean firing rates of two types of neurons change with the cue disparity, which shows that the activity of congruent neurons decreases with the disparity, whereas the activity of opposite neurons increases with the disparity, and they are equal at the disparity value of 90°.
evidence: This is shown in simulation results in Figure 7A

claim: The activity of opposite neurons increases with cue disparity.
source: Figure 7A displays how the mean firing rates of two types of neurons change with the cue disparity, which shows that the activity of congruent neurons decreases with the disparity, whereas the activity of opposite neurons increases with the disparity, and they are equal at the disparity value of 90°.
evidence: This is shown in simulation results in Figure 7A

claim: The brain can judge the validity of integration based on the competition between congruent and opposite neurons.
source: The brain can judge the validity of integration based on the competition between these two groups of neurons (see more remarks in Conclusions and Discussions).
evidence: This is proposed based on the complementary activities of the two neuron types

claim: Through combining the activities of congruent and opposite neurons, the neural system can recover the lost stimulus information from direct cues.
source: Thus, through combining the activities of congruent and opposite neurons, the neural system can recover the lost stimulus information from direct cues if necessary.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis and shown in Figure 7D

claim: Opposite neurons can discriminate cue disparity much finer than congruent neurons.
source: Indeed, the opposite neurons can discriminate the cue disparity much finer than congruent neurons (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in simulation results in Figure 8C

claim: Opposite neurons have been found in experiments for years but their functional role remains a mystery.
source: Opposite neurons have been found in experiments for years (Chen et al., 2013; Gu et al., 2008), but their functional role remains a mystery.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Two computational works explored the contribution of opposite neurons in inferring self-motion direction by eliminating confound information of object motion.
source: There have been few studies investigating this issue, and two computational works were reported (Kim et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2017), where the authors explored the contribution of opposite neurons in a computational task of inferring self-motion direction by eliminating the confound information of object motion.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous computational studies

claim: Previous studies showed that opposite neurons are essential as they provide complementary information to congruent neurons necessary to accomplish the required computation.
source: They showed that opposite neurons are essential, as they provide complementary information to congruent neurons necessary to accomplish the required computation.
evidence: This is based on findings from cited computational studies

claim: Opposite neurons are indispensable in multisensory processing.
source: This result is consistent with our idea that opposite neurons are indispensable in multisensory processing, but our study goes one step further by theoretically proposing that opposite neurons encode the disparity information between cues and that congruent and opposite neurons jointly realize concurrent multisensory processing.
evidence: This is proposed based on the model results and theoretical analysis

claim: The study has demonstrated that congruent neurons implement Bayesian cue integration within the framework of a single-component prior.
source: It is worthwhile to point out that in the present study, we have only demonstrated that congruent neurons implement Bayesian cue integration within the framework of a single-component prior and that opposite neurons encode the cue disparity information, and we have not explored whether they can combine together to realize a full Bayesian inference for multisensory processing.
evidence: This is a summary of what was demonstrated in the study

claim: The study has not explored whether congruent and opposite neurons can combine together to realize a full Bayesian inference for multisensory processing.
source: It is worthwhile to point out that in the present study, we have only demonstrated that congruent neurons implement Bayesian cue integration within the framework of a single-component prior and that opposite neurons encode the cue disparity information, and we have not explored whether they can combine together to realize a full Bayesian inference for multisensory processing.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study

claim: It is possible that opposite neurons can help the neural system to implement causal inference.
source: It is possible that opposite neurons, which encode the cue disparity information, can help the neural system to implement the causal inference.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions

claim: The model can be generalized to cases of processing more than two cues.
source: The present study only investigated integration and segregation of two sensory cues, but our model can be generalized to the cases of processing more than two cues that may happen in reality (Wozny et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a proposed extension of the model

claim: Opposite neurons, or their counterparts of similar functions, is a general characteristic of neural information processing where feature integration and segregation are involved.
source: In essence, the contribution of opposite neurons is to retain the disparity information between features to be integrated for the purpose of concurrent processing. We therefore expect that opposite neurons, or their counterparts of similar functions, is a general characteristic of neural information processing where feature integration and segregation are involved (Born, 2000; Thiele et al., 2002; Nadler et al., 2013; Goncalves and Welchman, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the model results and supported by citations

claim: In the visual system, there exist 'what not' detectors which respond best to discrepancies between cues and facilitate depth and shape perceptions.
source: Indeed, for example, it has been found in the visual system, there exist 'what not' detectors which respond best to discrepancies between cues (analogous to opposite neurons) and they facilitate depth and shape perceptions (Goncalves and Welchman, 2017; Rideaux and Welchman, 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental findings in the visual system

claim: The probabilistic model used in this study is widely adopted in multisensory research.
source: The probabilistic model used in this study is widely adopted in multisensory research (Bresciani et al., 2006; Ernst, 2006; Roach et al., 2006; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: The network consists of two reciprocally connected modules representing MSTd and VIP.
source: The neural circuit model we consider has the decentralized structure (Zhang et al., 2016), in the sense that it consists of two reciprocally connected modules (local processors), representing MSTd and VIP respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is the proposed model architecture shown in Figure 4A

claim: Each module has two groups of excitatory neurons with the same number: congruent and opposite neurons.
source: At each module, there exist two groups of excitatory neurons: congruent and opposite neurons (blue and red circles in Figure 4A respectively), and they have the same number of neurons, as supported by experiments (Figure 2C) (Chen et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is the model architecture supported by experimental data

claim: Each group of neurons is modeled as a continuous attractor neural network.
source: Each group of neurons is modeled as a continuous attractor neural network (CANN), mimicking the encoding of heading-direction in neural systems (Zhang, 1996; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is the modeling approach based on previous work

claim: The recurrent connection strength is not very strong to support persistent activities after switching off external stimuli, because no persistent activity is observed in multisensory areas.
source: In the model, the recurrent connection strength is not very strong to support persistent activities after switching off external stimuli, because no persistent activity is observed in multisensory areas.
evidence: This is a model design choice based on experimental observations

claim: Each network module contains 180 congruent and opposite neurons respectively in the simulation.
source: In our simulation, each network module contains 180 congruent and opposite neurons, respectively, whose preferred direction with respect to the feedforward cue is uniformly distributed in the feature space (−180°, 180°].
evidence: This is a simulation parameter
